title: The abnormal flags vanished at 15:00

injects.title: 19:00 The flags are gone
injects.text: A night nurse on 4 East asks why no lab result has shown a high or low flag since mid-afternoon. The interface log shows a change to the result feed was deployed at 15:00. About 600 results have been filed without abnormal flags across three units.

injects.title: 19:30 Shift change
injects.text: Your shift ends. The night informatics on-call, Sam, takes over the problem. Sam was not in the huddle.

injects.title: 20:30 Friction at the table
injects.text: The 4 East nurse manager says the lab should have caught it; the lab supervisor says nurses should read the values, not the flags. Two people have stopped talking.

injects.title: 22:00 A fix is ready
injects.text: The interface analyst has a corrected mapping and wants to deploy it now and go home.

objective: Structured communication and handoff tools such as SBAR, and why a handoff needs acknowledgment and a chance to ask questions
secondaryObjectives: TeamSTEPPS as an evidence-based framework for team communication, role clarity and safety
Scope of practice and roles of the health professions and other stakeholders, including patients
Team dynamics in solving complex health and health information problems

sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: SBAR 'stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation (or Request)', a structured way to share information about a condition or an issue that needs attention; the Recommendation step includes a repeat-back that 'repeats back the stated response ... to ensure accuracy'; starter phrases include 'Is there something I missed?'

sources.cite: AHRQ, CUSP Toolkit, Implement Teamwork and Communication
sources.note: Read 2026-11-17 through a summarizing fetch: a handoff is the 'Transfer of information, along with authority and responsibility', and each handoff 'includes an opportunity to ask questions, clarify, and confirm'; check-back is 'A strategy that ensures messages are received' (closed loop); a huddle 'Can be requested by any team member at any time'; briefings identify 'each team member's role and responsibilities'; TeamSTEPPS components are leadership, situation monitoring, mutual support and communication.
Every organization, person, count and time is invented teaching data; no real patient data is used. The case teaches the communication pattern, not lab values or treatment.

brief.situation: Tabletop exercise at Fairmount General Hospital (fictional). You are the clinical informatics analyst. At 19:00 a night nurse reports that lab results have stopped showing abnormal flags. You run the scenario with lab, nursing, pharmacy, a hospitalist lead and the night informatics on-call at the table.
handover: Change log: a result-feed mapping change was deployed at 15:00.
The hospital's interface-incident procedure says who fixes the interface; it says nothing about who tells the clinical teams.
howItWorks: Each inject arrives at its scenario time. Choose what you and the table do; each discussion takes scenario minutes.
Ask the table questions to find gaps in the procedure.
When you end the exercise, write the after-action report and explain your reasoning.

source.note: The facilitator ends the scenario at 23:00.

writeup.question: For the hot wash: how did the professions at the table work the problem, what nearly went wrong, and what changes before the next interface fault?

parts.label: Working across professions
parts.criteria: A huddle with every profession that owns part of the risk (lab, nursing, pharmacy, a physician lead, informatics), an SBAR so each hears the same picture, named roles for the review, and a shared goal restated when friction rose, with cause left for the after-action.
parts.modelAnswer: At 19:00 we huddled with the lab, nursing, pharmacy and the hospitalist lead and gave an SBAR. The lab phoned abnormal results since 15:00 with read-back, nursing confirmed each patient, pharmacy checked dependent orders, the hospitalist decided who needed review. When leads clashed we restated the goal and left blame for later.

parts.label: The handoff
parts.criteria: A handoff transfers responsibility, so it needs structure (SBAR), acknowledgment (read-back) and a chance to ask questions; a chat message with a ticket number transfers none of that.
parts.modelAnswer: I called Sam with an SBAR; Sam read back the plan and asked who to call if the lab list ran late. A chat message would have left Sam not knowing who was doing what.

parts.label: What changes
parts.criteria: Gaps found by asking the table, each with an owner and date: who notifies clinical teams of interface faults, a named overnight clinical contact, and an SBAR template in the on-call kit; the fix deployed only after lab verification.
parts.modelAnswer: Three gaps, each owned with a date: notification duty added to the procedure, an overnight clinical contact named, and an SBAR template in the kit. The fix went in after the lab verified flags.

unreviewed.headline: Results went unreviewed
unreviewed.body: An interface fault is a clinical problem: the people who act on results must hear about it, not only the people who fix the feed.

droppedHandoff.headline: The handoff dropped the plan
droppedHandoff.body: A handoff transfers responsibility. Without structure, read-back and a chance to ask questions, the next person starts from a ticket number.

scoring.modelReasoning: An interface fault that strips abnormal flags is a clinical risk that crosses professions: the lab produces results, nurses and physicians act on them, pharmacy checks orders that depend on them, and informatics owns the feed. So huddle at once with all of them and give one SBAR, and agree who reviews the 600 unflagged results. At shift change, hand off by SBAR with read-back and a chance to ask questions, because a handoff transfers responsibility. When leads clash, restate the shared goal and name each role; cause belongs in the after-action. Deploy the fix only after the lab verifies flags on test patients. Then give each gap the table found an owner and a date.
